column1: # The cells of PLAN.md item 1, and what each is predicted to do. Tab-separated;
# `#` comments and blank lines ignored. run.sh measures each and fails on any cell
# whose measured verdict differs from `expect` — in *either* direction, because a
# prediction that turns out too pessimistic is as much a finding as one too optimistic.
# `expect` is `survives` or `dies`: whether the session created in one SSH login is
# still there in the next, after the first has been logged out.
# nomux reads none of these axes any more. `spawn` launches the daemon directly and
# always, so the daemon lands in whatever cgroup its login already had, and the only axis
# that can decide its fate is KillUserProcesses — which is a host policy nomux never sees.
# `pam_systemd` decides whether there is a login session to be in at all, and `linger` is
# kept precisely because it is now predicted to change nothing: it used to be the axis that
# turned `dies` into `survives`, and a cell that measures it no longer doing so is what
# would catch a scope launch coming back. `logout` is an axis of a different kind — not how
# the host is configured but how the login ends, `clean` for an orderly `ssh host 'cmd'`
# return and `abrupt` for a connection blackholed at the wire. See run.sh's `abrupt_login`.
# cell
# No pam_systemd: no session scope, no $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, no user bus. Nothing on the host
# is managing logins, so the daemon inherits sshd's own unit and nothing kills it whatever
# KillUserProcesses says.
no-user-bus
# The forgiving host, and the one most distributions ship: the daemon is left in the login
# session's scope and the session scope is not killed at logout.
kup-off-linger-off
# Linger on, and it makes no difference: a lingering `user@UID.service` owns nothing the
# daemon is in, and nothing would have killed it here anyway. The control for the pair
# below — it says a `survives` under linger is not evidence linger did anything.
kup-off-linger-on
# The cell the whole exercise is for. The daemon is launched directly into
# `session-N.scope`, and logind kills that scope's contents at the final logout.
kup-on-linger-off
# Predicted `dies`, and this row is the deletion's own regression test. It recorded
# `survives` while `spawn` detected a lingering user manager and launched through
# `systemd-run --user --scope`, which put the daemon in a manager-owned transient scope
# outside the login session. That launcher is gone, so linger now buys nothing: the daemon
# is in `session-N.scope` like its linger-off twin and dies with it. A `survives` measured
# here again would mean a scope launch had come back into the product.
kup-on-linger-on
# The same five hosts, logged out of by having the network taken away rather than by
# saying goodbye — the case nomux exists for, and the one teardown path the clean half
# cannot reach. sshd learns of it only when `ClientAliveInterval` expires, and reaches the
# logout through `cleanup_exit` rather than through an orderly channel close.
# All five are predicted to repeat their clean twin's verdict, and the prediction is a
# claim about *where* the two paths converge rather than a guess that nothing differs.
# What sshd does differently is only how it learns the client has gone; what it does next
# — PAM's `session close`, so pam_systemd's release of the session, so logind stopping
# `session-N.scope` and applying KillUserProcesses to whatever is still in it — is the
# same code on both paths. So the daemon's fate should turn on the cgroup it is in and
# nothing else, exactly as in the clean half.
# A deviation here would be the more interesting result of the two: it would mean sshd's
# timeout path skips a teardown step the orderly path takes, and that `survives` on a
# clean logout is not the promise nomux is actually making to a dropped connection.
drop-no-user-bus
drop-kup-off-linger-off
drop-kup-off-linger-on
drop-kup-on-linger-off
drop-kup-on-linger-on
